title: Putting Ibsen’s characters on trial
gist: A review of 'A Trial – after An Enemy of the People', Christiane Jatahy's Brazilian stage sequel to Ibsen that put Wagner Moura's whistleblowing doctor on trial before a nightly audience jury; the critic finds the production dramatically compelling but ultimately unpersuasive once she discovers the supposedly spontaneous jury questions were actually scripted.

insights.claim: Christiane Jatahy, director of 'A Trial – after An Enemy of the People' which opened this year's Edinburgh International Festival, was born under the Brazilian military dictatorship of the late 1960s and lived through Jair Bolsonaro's presidency, which weakened protections for indigenous groups and accelerated Amazon deforestation.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Grounds the director's political sensibility and choice of source material in her personal history under authoritarian rule.
insights.quote: Christiane Jatahy, the director of A Trial – after An Enemy of the People, which opened this year’s Edinburgh International Festival, was born under the Brazilian military dictatorship of the late 1960s.

insights.claim: Jatahy was awarded the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the 2022 Venice Biennale, with a citation describing her as 'a harsh and acute observer of the violent cruelty of our world'.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Establishes Jatahy's international standing and thematic reputation prior to this production.
insights.quote: In 2022, when she was awarded the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the Venice Biennale, the citation described her as “a harsh and acute observer of the violent cruelty of our world”.

insights.claim: Working with screenwriter Lucas Paraizo and Oscar-nominated actor Wagner Moura, Jatahy staged a trial Ibsen never wrote, putting Thomas Stockmann — the whistleblowing doctor from Ibsen's 1882 An Enemy of the People — on trial in an attempt to clear his name, adding themes of vested interests, political hypocrisy, sibling rivalry and family alienation.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Describes the specific dramaturgical intervention: a sequel/trial narrative grafted onto a 19th-century Ibsen play.
insights.quote: Working with screenwriter Lucas Paraizo and Oscar-nominated actor Wagner Moura to put the poor man on trial in an attempt to clear his name, Jatahy has woven an altogether modern tale about vested interests, political hypocrisy, sibling rivalry and family alienation.

insights.claim: The production mixes video, onstage drama performed in Portuguese, and occasional asides to the audience in English, with 11 audience members called up each night to sit at the back of the stage and act as a jury deciding whether the defendant is an enemy of the people.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
entities: A Trial – after An Enemy of the People
insights.so_what: Describes the core interactive conceit that distinguishes this production and drives the reviewer's later critique.
insights.quote: Eleven members of the audience are called up each night to sit at the back of the stage and act as a jury. They are told that they will decide whether or not the defendant is indeed an enemy of the people.

insights.claim: The plot's central pollution allegation involves hexavalent chromium (chromium-6) leaking from a nearby tanning factory into the resort town's water supply, with Stockmann's character citing Erin Brockovich (2000), in which the same poison appears, and Jaws (1975), where a shark threatens a summer of swimming.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Shows how the production updates Ibsen's 19th-century pollution plot with a specific, real-world-recognisable toxin and pop-culture references for the audience.
insights.quote: the water is being polluted by hexavalent chromium, a toxic form of the heavy metal chromium, also known as chromium-6, which is leaking from a nearby tanning factory

insights.claim: Wagner Moura plays Stockmann as a shouty, opinionated and unwavering defendant of the truth, insisting the spa resort must close even if repairs take two years and there is no public money available.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Characterises the lead performance that anchors the production's emotional and moral centre.
insights.quote: Moura ... is here a shouty, opinionated and unwavering defendant of the truth: that the water is being polluted by hexavalent chromium ... He insists the spa resort must be closed even if it takes two years to repair and there is no public money available to do the work.

insights.claim: Julia Bernat plays Petra, Stockmann's oldest child and spokesperson for the defence, as fierce and brittle, having lost her home and watched her mother die, partly from depression caused by her father's intransigent focus on the pollution cause.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Adds the emotional/family-collapse subplot that gives the trial personal stakes beyond the pollution case itself.
insights.quote: Julia Bernat as Petra, Stockmann’s oldest child and spokesperson for the defence, is both fierce and brittle.

insights.claim: In a key scene, Petra tells the audience directly, in a personal aside outside the formal defence, 'I don't need to be defended or protected. That is just the hierarchy that you want to protect.'
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Highlights a standout moment where the production breaks from its trial structure to deliver a direct, personal statement.
insights.quote: “I don’t need to be defended or protected. That is just the hierarchy that you want to protect.”

insights.claim: Danilo Grangheia, playing Stockmann's brother Peter, the former mayor and prosecutor, brings the play its real depth as a 'creepy yet plangent' figure who claims to be his brother's saviour while ignoring his own bullying of a local newspaper editor and skating over a thin, self-serving scientific report.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
insights.so_what: Identifies the antagonist performance the reviewer singles out as the production's most layered.
insights.quote: it is Danilo Grangheia as that brother who brings the play its real depth: creepy yet plangent, he makes a good case for himself as the saviour of the people

insights.claim: In his final speech, Stockmann tells the jury: 'The truth is over ... that means there are no longer facts, there are only versions ... If my reality is so different from yours, then we live in different worlds.'
insights.speaker: Wagner Moura
insights.so_what: Captures the production's thematic core about the collapse of shared truth, a resonant line for a post-truth political era.
insights.quote: “The truth is over,” Stockmann tells the jury in his final speech. “That scares me because that means there are no longer facts, there are only versions. All of this becomes just a staging. If my reality is so different from yours, then we live in different worlds.”

themes.theme: The critic's verdict: a scripted jury

insights.claim: Having seen the play twice — once as a jury member and once in the main audience — the reviewer discovered that the questions each night's jury supposedly asked the prosecutor and defendant were not spontaneous but were actually part of the scripted text.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
entities: A Trial – after An Enemy of the People
insights.so_what: Undermines the production's central interactive premise, revealing the audience-participation device as staged rather than genuine.
insights.quote: I saw it twice—once as a member of the jury and once in the main audience—and quickly realised that the questions each night’s jury supposedly put to both prosecutor and defendant didn’t come from the jury at all; they were part of the script.

insights.claim: The jury's vote was 8–3 on both nights the reviewer attended, finding the defendant was not an enemy of the people, a result she calls 'too obvious and too neat', concluding the jury functioned only as a stage device rather than as genuine audience representatives.
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
entities: A Trial – after An Enemy of the People
insights.so_what: Delivers the reviewer's final critical judgment: the production's most ambitious formal device was ultimately hollow.
insights.quote: There was no debate among the jurors when they went offstage, and the vote—8–3 on both nights, finding that the hero was not an enemy of the people—was both too obvious and too neat. So the jury ... turned out to be just a stage device.
insights.locator: There was no debate among the jurors

insights.claim: The reviewer's overall assessment is that the play was 'certainly dramatic, but not entirely persuasive', echoing Moura's own onstage line distinguishing theatre from film: 'This is not a movie. It's theatre.'
insights.speaker: Fiammetta Rocco
entities: A Trial – after An Enemy of the People
insights.so_what: Summarises the review's final verdict on the production's overall success.
insights.quote: It was certainly dramatic, but not entirely persuasive.
